title: Jizo by the road
hookLine: in Japan Ksitigarbha is Jizo, protector of travelers and of children who have died

lines: A STONE FIGURE BY A PATH.
A RED CAP, A RED BIB.
cards: A small stone figure stands at the edge of a mountain path in Japan. Round, shaved head. Eyes half closed.
Someone has tied a red bib around its neck and put a knitted red cap on its head, carefully, the way you'd dress a toddler for cold weather.
There's a coin at its feet, an orange, and a plastic pinwheel turning in the wind. Nobody is around. This is yesterday's bodhisattva, under the name Japanese Buddhists know him by.

teach.b: Jizo is the Japanese way of reading the name Ksitigarbha, as it was written in Chinese. Same bodhisattva, same vow to go into the low places.
But in Japan he has come down to the side of the road: small, close, easy to reach. He's a protector of travelers.

Jizo figures stand at crossroads, along paths, at the edges of villages and mountain passes, where people come and go and a journey can turn. A traveler can stop, bow, leave something small, and walk on.
And he's a protector of children, especially children who have died. This is where yesterday's vow becomes very tender. There's a story people tell, carried in old Japanese hymns.
Children who die young go to a riverbank in the next world, where they pile up little towers of stones as offerings for the parents they left behind. Demons come and knock the towers down.

teach.h: A BIB TIED ON BY HAND.

teach.b: He gathers the children up, hides them in the sleeves of his robe, and keeps them safe. So parents who have lost a child, including a pregnancy that ended too soon, sometimes come to a Jizo figure to remember.

They tie on the bib, set down a toy, stack a few stones. Some say the red cloth is for protection, others that it simply dresses him like a child; the meanings vary from place to place. Each one is an act of care.
A vow from a sutra, about suffering in the lowest places, has become a stone figure you can kneel beside, small enough to dress with your own hands.

how: In Japan, people leave offerings at Jizo figures by roads and in temple grounds, and some temples hold memorial rites in which parents who have lost a child or a pregnancy dress Jizo figures in red bibs and caps.

o: a stone lantern set beside temple paths in Japan
Ksitigarbha as Japan knows him, guardian of children
a Japanese god of mountains who guards the harvest

games.q: on the riverbank, the children's stone towers keep getting knocked down. what does Jizo do?
o: gathers the children into his sleeves.
sends them back to their parents.
games.why: in the story people tell, Jizo comes, gathers the children up, and hides them in the sleeves of his robe.

practice: Bring to mind a small roadside shrine you know: a memorial by a road, flowers tied to a fence, a plaque on a bench, a statue in a garden. Think of whoever put it there and whoever it's for, without needing to know their names.
If you'd like, imagine setting one small stone beside it.

wordCard.voice: Jizo. Ksitigarbha as Japan knows him: the small figure by the road, guardian of travelers and of children who have died. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: Jizo, written with the Chinese characters for Ksitigarbha, often rendered earth store.

carryVoice: Your line: the protector of children. If a loss feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Until tomorrow, gently.

sources.ref: Japanese Jizo devotion; the riverbank (Sai no Kawara) hymns
